\section[o docente]{o docente — the lecturer, the teacher}

\label{lesson:PT-C377-docente}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the semester, then the Portuguese for the tuition fee.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o docente}
\textbf{o docente} — \textquotedblleft{}the lecturer, the teacher\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Os docentes desta faculdade são muito exigentes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The lecturers at this faculty are very demanding.}
\end{quote}

Formal; \emph{o corpo docente} — the teaching staff.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{docente} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{docēns} \textquotedblleft{}teaching\textquotedblright{}, the present participle of \emph{docēre} \textquotedblleft{}to teach, to instruct\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o docente}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o docente}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o docente}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the semester, then the Portuguese for the tuition fee, then say \emph{o docente} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o docente mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The lecturer, the teacher\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[o orientador]{o orientador — the thesis supervisor}

\label{lesson:PT-C377-orientador}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the tuition fee, then the Portuguese for the lecturer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o orientador}
\textbf{o orientador} — \textquotedblleft{}the thesis supervisor\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O meu orientador lê tudo o que escrevo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My supervisor reads everything I write.}
\end{quote}

Feminine \emph{a orientadora}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{orientador} is built on \emph{orientar} \textquotedblleft{}to guide\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{oriente} \textquotedblleft{}east\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{oriēns} \textquotedblleft{}rising (sun)\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{orīrī} \textquotedblleft{}to rise\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): to find the east is to find your way.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[a bolsa de estudo]{a bolsa de estudo — the scholarship, the grant}

\label{lesson:PT-C377-bolsa-de-estudo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the lecturer, then the Portuguese for the thesis supervisor.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a bolsa de estudo}
\textbf{a bolsa de estudo} — \textquotedblleft{}the scholarship, the grant\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ela recebeu uma bolsa de estudo para estudar fora.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She got a scholarship to study abroad.}
\end{quote}

\emph{O bolseiro} — the grant holder (in Brazil \emph{o bolsista}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{bolsa} \textquotedblleft{}purse\textquotedblright{} goes back through Old Portuguese \emph{bolssa} to Late Latin \emph{bursa} \textquotedblleft{}oxhide, purse\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), usually traced to Greek \emph{býrsa} \textquotedblleft{}hide\textquotedblright{}; \emph{estudo} is inherited from Latin \emph{studium} \textquotedblleft{}zeal, eagerness, study\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[o mestrado]{o mestrado — the master's degree}

\label{lesson:PT-C377-mestrado}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the thesis supervisor, then the Portuguese for the scholarship.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o mestrado}
\textbf{o mestrado} — \textquotedblleft{}the master's degree\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ele está a fazer um mestrado em engenharia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He is doing a master's degree in engineering.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Fazer um mestrado} — to do a master's.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mestrado} is built on \emph{mestre} \textquotedblleft{}master\textquotedblright{} with \emph{-ado} (EtymDB); \emph{mestre} is inherited from Latin \emph{magister} \textquotedblleft{}master, teacher\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[o doutoramento]{o doutoramento — the doctorate, the PhD}

\label{lesson:PT-C377-doutoramento}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the scholarship, then the Portuguese for the master's degree.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o doutoramento}
\textbf{o doutoramento} — \textquotedblleft{}the doctorate, the PhD\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O doutoramento demora pelo menos três anos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The doctorate takes at least three years.}
\end{quote}

European Portuguese; in Brazil \emph{o doutorado}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{doutoramento} is built on \emph{doutorar} \textquotedblleft{}to award a doctorate\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{doutor}, inherited from Latin \emph{doctor} \textquotedblleft{}a teacher, an instructor\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), on \emph{docēre} \textquotedblleft{}to teach\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
